article.overview: An environmental monitoring station is a surface instrument package that records the conditions around it over time, rather than investigating one specific object or process. On the Moon, such a station can measure the radiation environment, charged particles (plasma) near the surface, the very thin neutral gas envelope, and surface thermal behaviour. The catalogue name is generic. There is no single standard design for this class, and the examples in this article differ widely in purpose, age and status. The article first describes the class, then separates the flown examples from the proposed one.
article.description: Environmental monitoring stations are built around one or more sensors that track a changing environmental quantity. The lunar surface has extreme day-night temperature swings, exposure to solar wind, cosmic rays and solar energetic particles, and only a very thin gas envelope, so each quantity needs its own sensor design. A station usually combines a sensor head (or several), electronics that condition and digitise the signal, a time reference, thermal control, a power source and a data link to Earth. Data are normally recorded as counts, spectra or time series so that scientists can follow changes across the lunar day and over longer periods. A single station measures conditions at one point, so its value comes from long records and from comparison with other stations or orbital observations.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a lunar environmental station is to characterise the conditions that will affect science, engineering and eventually human exploration. Radiation measurements inform shielding for crews and equipment, and they test models of how cosmic rays and solar particles interact with the regolith. Plasma and neutral-gas measurements show how the solar wind and ultraviolet light interact with the surface and its tenuous atmosphere. Temperature records support thermal design and help scientists understand how the regolith stores and releases heat. Long records also separate persistent conditions from short-lived events.
article.operating_principle: The operating principle depends on the quantity being measured. Charged particles can be sorted by energy and mass using electric and magnetic fields, and then counted by a channel electron multiplier, which produces an electrical pulse for each particle that reaches it. Solid-state detectors, such as silicon detectors, produce a signal when radiation deposits energy in them, and segmenting the detector lets the instrument tell which region was hit. A Langmuir probe is a conducting electrode placed in a plasma. By sweeping its voltage and measuring the current it collects, the probe gives estimates of electron and ion density and energy. A cold cathode gauge is a type of pressure gauge; in general terms, it relates a discharge current to gas density, although the Apollo source consulted here does not describe its sensing technology. In every case the raw output must be calibrated, corrected for electronics temperature, and interpreted using the instrument's known geometry.
article.scientific_importance: Environmental stations provide ground truth. Orbital instruments and transport models can estimate surface conditions, but direct measurements test those estimates. The Chang'E-4 Lunar Lander Neutron and Dosimetry (LND) paper states that the knowledge of the lunar surface radiation environment was then based exclusively on calculations using radiation transport models, which made surface measurements a central motivation for the instrument. Plasma measured close to the surface, away from the lander body, gives information that an orbiter cannot easily provide. The Apollo ALSEP experience also showed that surface stations can return useful records for years when their power and thermal design allow it.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for an environmental monitoring station. The examples below are specific instruments or a specific proposed station, and each value is tied to that example. Values not found in the fetched sources are marked as not stated. No images are embedded in this article: no direct image asset URL was verified during this run, so the source pages are linked instead.

examples.name: Apollo ALSEP Suprathermal Ion Detector Experiment (SIDE) and Cold Cathode Gauge Experiment (CCGE)
examples.type: Historical lunar surface instrument package (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)
examples.status: Flown and operated on the Moon. Deployed by Apollo astronauts from 1969.
examples.narrative: The Suprathermal Ion Detector Experiment measured the energy and mass of positive ions produced near the lunar surface by solar wind or ultraviolet ionisation of gases. The Cold Cathode Gauge Experiment was carried in a SIDE compartment and aimed to measure the density, not the composition, of the Moon's tenuous atmosphere. Both were part of the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), which was arranged around a central station. The SIDE was deployed about 15 m from the central station, according to the Apollo 12 instrument description.

facts.label: Sensor configuration (SIDE)
facts.value: Mass analyser: Wien filter in tandem with a curved-plate electrostatic energy-per-charge filter, followed by a channel electron multiplier used as an ion counter. Total Ion Detector: channel electron multiplier without a velocity filter.

facts.label: Measurement ranges (SIDE)
facts.value: Mass analyser: 20 mass channels covering approximately 10 to 1000 amu per charge, at six energies (0.2, 0.6, 1.8, 5.4, 16.2 and 48.6 eV). Only the two highest energies had dependable laboratory calibrations for Apollo 12. Total Ion Detector: 20 energy steps from 10 to 3500 eV.

facts.label: Cadence (SIDE)
facts.value: One mass spectrum and one energy spectrum every 24 s in normal mode. Multiplier bias -3.5 kV at the input ends.

facts.label: Thermal control
facts.value: Switched on and off for several days on each side of lunar noon to keep internal temperatures below about 55 degrees C, per the Apollo 12 instrument description.

facts.label: Operating dates (SIDE)
facts.value: Switched on 19 November 1969 at 19:45 UT. Lunar-night standby from 18 January 1976. Switched off 3 May 1976 because there was insufficient power for all ALSEP instruments.

facts.label: CCGE operating dates
facts.value: Not stated in the fetched source.

facts.label: Reported CCGE result (secondary, not verified)
facts.value: A secondary summary of the Cold Cathode Gauge Experiment reports a nighttime atmospheric density of about 2 x 10^11 particles per cubic metre measured on Apollo 14 and 15, which was attributed to gas freezing out at low temperature. This was seen only in a search summary and has not been checked against the primary Apollo reports.

facts.label: Mass and power
facts.value: Not stated in the fetched source for either instrument.

facts.label: Deployment context
facts.value: ALSEP was placed by astronauts and connected to the central station by power and control cables.

examples.name: Chang'E-4 Lunar Lander Neutron and Dosimetry (LND) experiment
examples.status: Flown. Lander and rover launched 7 December 2018; the lander landed on 3 January 2019 on the lunar far side, as described in the LND paper.
examples.narrative: The LND measures neutron and gamma radiation produced when cosmic rays and solar particles interact with the lunar soil, and it records charged-particle and neutral-particle spectra. The paper describes thermal neutrons as a sensitive indicator of subsurface water content. Its detector stack uses ten segmented silicon solid-state detectors. The sensor head is separate from the electronics box so that the sensor can stay cooler in the lander's thermal environment.

facts.label: Detectors
facts.value: Ten segmented silicon solid-state detectors (A to J), each nominally 500 micrometres thick. Measured thicknesses (paper Table 1) were 502 to 514 micrometres.

facts.label: Segmentation and field of view
facts.value: Inner and outer segments of roughly equal area (inner 440 mm^2, outer 435.6 mm^2). Full opening angle 29.4 degrees, pointed about 13 degrees from the lander deck normal.

facts.label: Thermal neutron efficiency
facts.value: About 1/50, from laboratory calibration at ATI Vienna in September 2017 (measured in the laboratory, not on the Moon).

facts.label: Time resolution
facts.value: Up to 1 minute for dose, LET, charged-particle and neutral spectra; 10 minutes for thermal neutrons; 1 hour for the full summary product.

facts.label: Electronics
facts.value: 20 preamplifiers and 30 shaper/ADC pairs (design values).

facts.label: Lander opening
facts.value: 16 cm x 23 cm window in the lander's top panel (design value).

facts.label: Measured flight temperatures
facts.value: First lunar day sensor-head temperatures reported from -7.97 to 48.10 degrees C, with the highest values on the sensor-head analogue board. Taken from the arXiv full text; the figure should be rechecked against the published paper before citation.

facts.label: Reported dose results (secondary coverage, not verified against primary paper)
facts.value: Zhang et al. (2020) are reported in secondary coverage as giving an average dose equivalent of about 1,369 microsieverts per day, with an additional 208 microsieverts per day from protons during South Atlantic Anomaly crossings. A search summary of the abstract gives an average absorbed dose rate in silicon of 13.2 +/- 1 microgray per hour and a neutral-particle dose rate of 3.1 +/- 0.5 microgray per hour. These values have not been checked against the primary paper.

facts.label: Model-based expectations (not flight measurements)
facts.value: The paper gives about 1.3 counts per second of neutral-particle events in one detector channel without RTG and RHU background, and about 0.06 neutron counts per second above about 1 MeV compared with about 0.006 gamma counts per second. These are model expectations, not measured lunar values.

facts.label: Mass, power and sensor-head dimensions
facts.value: Not stated in the fetched text.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-3 RAMBHA-LP (Radio Anatomy of Moon Bound Hypersensitive ionosphere and Atmosphere - Langmuir Probe)
examples.status: Flown on the Chandrayaan-3 lander in 2023. Results described by ISRO as an initial assessment.
examples.narrative: RAMBHA-LP is a Langmuir probe that measures the electron and ion density and energy of the plasma near the lunar surface. It was mounted on the lander's upper deck and released by a hold-release mechanism after touchdown. The 1 m boom keeps the probe in plasma that is not disturbed by the lander body, according to ISRO.

facts.label: Probe
facts.value: 5 cm metallic spherical probe on a 1 m boom.

facts.label: Sweep
facts.value: Bias from -12 V to +12 V in 0.1 V increments; dwell time of 1 millisecond.

facts.label: Current sensitivity
facts.value: Detects return currents as low as picoamperes.

facts.label: Measured near-surface density (ISRO initial assessment, page dated 31 August 2023)
facts.value: Approximately 5 to 30 million electrons per cubic metre during the early lunar daytime. ISRO describes the plasma as relatively sparse and the result as initial, so it should be treated as preliminary.

facts.label: Mass, dimensions and power
facts.value: Not stated on the fetched ISRO page.

facts.label: Unresolved discrepancy
facts.value: A later ISRO ground-truth page, seen only as a search summary, reports electron densities of about 380 to 600 per cubic centimetre for 23 August to 3 September 2023. That is in different units and far above the earlier figure. The gap is unexplained in the sources consulted, so no later density is adopted here.

examples.dimensions: probe 5 cm diameter (sphere); boom about 1 m; other dimensions not stated

examples.name: NASA Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS)
examples.status: Not flown according to the fetched NASA page. The page describes an engineering unit that has been built and tested and states that the station is one of the first three payloads on Artemis III.
examples.narrative: NASA's Goddard Engineering and Technology Directorate describes LEMS as a compact, autonomous seismometer suite for continuous, long-term monitoring of the seismic environment near the lunar south polar region. Its purpose overlaps with the passive seismometer payload, so it is included here as a monitoring station rather than as a separate seismic design. The fetched page does not name its individual instruments or state its power method.

facts.label: Engineering unit testing
facts.value: An engineering unit was vibration-tested to simulate launch and landing stresses and was exposed to ultra-high vacuum and harsh thermal conditions simulating the lunar surface, according to the NASA page.

facts.label: Intended operating duration
facts.value: From three months up to two years on the lunar surface, according to the NASA page.

facts.label: Manifest statement
facts.value: The NASA page states that LEMS is one of the first three payloads on Artemis III and that Artemis III is currently planned to launch in 2027. The page was last updated on 2 June 2026 and carries a notice that NASA is not updating it during a federal funding lapse, so the schedule may be out of date.

facts.label: Instrument list
facts.value: Not named on the fetched NASA page. Search summaries of other sources list different instrument sets. These lists conflict with each other and are not used here.

facts.label: Mass, dimensions and power
facts.value: Not stated on the fetched NASA page.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not a useful basis for comparison across this class. The examples range from an Apollo-era experiment that shared an ALSEP central station to a lander-mounted detector stack and a boom-mounted probe. Where dimensions are stated, they describe a specific sensor head, not a whole station.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass and power are not publicly specified for most examples in the sources consulted. For the Chang'E-4 LND and the Chandrayaan-3 RAMBHA-LP, the fetched sources state no mass or power. For the NASA LEMS, the fetched page states no mass or power either. Mass should therefore not be inferred for this payload class without a named instrument and a primary source.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is a real constraint. The Apollo SIDE experiment was switched off on 3 May 1976 because there was insufficient power for all ALSEP instruments, as recorded in the Apollo 12 ALSEP instrument description. The power source and lunar-night power method for the LEMS are not stated on its fetched NASA page.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar environmental station must survive vacuum, extreme thermal cycling, radiation and micrometeoroid impacts. Thermal control is a recurring design issue. The Apollo SIDE was switched on and off for several days around each lunar noon to keep its internal temperatures below about 55 degrees C. The Chang'E-4 LND sensor head was separated from its electronics so that it could run cooler, and its sensor-head temperatures during the first lunar day were reported from about -8 degrees C to 48 degrees C. Power and the lunar night matter as well. The SIDE stopped in 1976 when power was insufficient for all ALSEP instruments. Installation also affects the measurement. RAMBHA-LP uses a 1 m boom so that its probe samples undisturbed plasma away from the lander body. Operationally, a station also needs a reliable time reference, a data path to Earth and a stable mounting.
article.limitations: A single station is a point measurement and cannot map spatial variation across the surface. Results depend on calibration, instrument geometry (for example, field of view and shielding) and the temperature of the electronics. Power loss, thermal cycling and component failure limit lifetime, as the Apollo SIDE shows. Several values in this article are preliminary (the RAMBHA-LP initial assessment), secondary (the LND dose values and the CCGE nighttime density), or unresolved (the RAMBHA-LP later density). Instrument-level values must not be mixed with mission-level values or with targets.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: An environmental monitoring station is a surface payload. It can be a dedicated station, a component of a larger lander payload, or an instrument that astronauts place on the surface. The examples show three approaches: astronaut placement and cabling (ALSEP), fixed integration into a lander (LND), and mechanical deployment after touchdown (RAMBHA-LP).
transportation_process: Integrate the station, its power and its data interfaces with the lander or with the astronaut deployment plan on Earth.
Launch the lander or spacecraft and transfer it toward the Moon.
Land the payload, or carry it to the surface for astronaut placement.
Deploy the sensor head or boom, or place the station on a stable surface.
Level and thermally protect the station, connect power and data, and commission and calibrate the instruments.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: ALSEP instruments were placed by astronauts and cabled to the central station, with the SIDE about 15 m from it. RAMBHA-LP was mounted on the lander deck and released by a hold-release mechanism after touchdown. LND was mounted in the lander behind a 16 cm x 23 cm window in the top panel; the fetched text does not describe a separate deployment step. The LEMS deployment method is not stated on the fetched NASA page.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Three flown examples are discussed here: the Apollo ALSEP SIDE and CCGE, which operated from 1969 to 1976 for the SIDE; the Chang'E-4 LND, which operated from its 2019 landing; and the Chandrayaan-3 RAMBHA-LP, which operated in 2023. The LEMS is a proposed example with a planned Artemis III manifest statement.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: NASA states that LEMS is one of the first three payloads on Artemis III, but the fetched page does not name the lander or its interfaces. No compatibility with a named lander has been verified for any example in this article. Compatibility should not be inferred from mass or size, because those values are missing for most examples.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo ALSEP was a package of geophysical and environmental instruments around a central station, and the SIDE and CCGE were among its environmental experiments. The LND paper describes its experiment as the first active dosimetry measurement on the lunar surface, in place of surface values that had been calculated. RAMBHA-LP produced early plasma measurements from the Chandrayaan-3 lander. Together these examples show that surface environmental data are scientifically valuable, but each is a record from one place and one instrument.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Environmental monitoring station is a generic catalogue name, so this article covers a class rather than one design. The RAMBHA-LP density value is an initial assessment, and a later value in different units could not be reconciled from the sources consulted. The LND dose rates are secondary-source values that were not checked against the primary paper. The CCGE nighttime density comes from a secondary summary. The LEMS instrument list conflicts across sources and is not confirmed, and the NASA page carries a funding-lapse notice. Mass and power are missing for most examples. No images were verified, so the article has no embedded images.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue ID 315, name 'Environmental monitoring station' and category 16 'Calibration, reference and monitoring systems' were confirmed against lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.
No images are included. No direct image asset URL was verified in this run, so image arrays are empty and all source pages are linked in the references.

The LND dose values (1,369 microsieverts per day; 208 microsieverts per day SAA; 13.2 and 3.1 microgray per hour) come from secondary coverage and a search summary. The primary paper (Science Advances, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aaz1334) returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
The LND flight temperature range (-7.97 to 48.10 degrees C) was taken from the arXiv full text as extracted by the reading tool, and should be rechecked against the published paper before citation.

The RAMBHA-LP later ISRO density (380 to 600 per cubic centimetre, 23 August to 3 September 2023) was seen only in a search summary. It conflicts in units and magnitude with the initial ISRO value (5 to 30 million per cubic metre). It is recorded as unresolved and not adopted.
The RAMBHA-LP electron temperature (3,000 to 8,000 K) was seen only in a search summary and was not verified, so it is omitted.
The LEMS instrument lists in search summaries conflict with one another and with the NASA page, which names no instruments. None are adopted.
The NASA ALSEP overview page fetched in this run did not contain ALSEP content, so ALSEP facts come from the PDS Apollo 12 instrument description and secondary summaries.
The PubMed page for PMID 32978156 returned a cookie notice and was not verified as the Zhang et al. paper.
Mass, power and sensor-head dimensions are not stated in the fetched sources for any example. They are recorded as null rather than estimated.
